content:
As one of the most popular wines on the market, Sauvignon Blanc takes up plenty of shelf space in stores. And between the powerhouse Savvy B-producing region of Marlborough, New Zealand and the always-popular Sancerre, most of that space is dedicated to the heavy-hitting brands and regions. But there are great wines to discover beyond the big names, whether you’re a fan of the grape’s lean, mineral-driven side or the bolder expressions brimming with passion fruit and jalapeño.

It’s easy for wine lovers to gravitate toward an old reliable, but with such a wide variety of expressions, it’s well worth diving into the world of Sauvignon Blanc to uncover its hidden gems. To figure out which bottles deserve a little more love, we asked 10 sommeliers to name the most underrated Sauvignon Blanc on the market right now. From sleeper Loire Valley sub-regions to unsung producers in Austria, here’s what they said.

The most underrated Sauvignon Blanc, according to sommeliers:

  • Casa Jipi Sauvignon Blanc
  • Hannes Sabathi Sauvignon Blanc
  • Sandy Cove Sauvignon Blanc
  • Domaine du Salvard Cheverny Blanc 2024
  • Sancerre Domaine Hippolyte Reverdy 2025
  • Sauvignon Blanc from Quincy
  • Pepper Bridge Winery Sauvignon Blanc
  • Paul Clüver Sauvignon Blanc 2025
  • Domaine Pellé Menetou-Salon Morogues Les Blanchais 2023
  • Domaine Durand Sancerre

“I really like Casa Jipi Sauvignon Blanc from Baja and their awesome winemaker, Lulu Martinez. It is a little fuller — but still fresh and crisp — and has great melon and fresh jalapeño notes. The citrus runs to orange, and it has an amazing salinity that brings a little curd out of the grapefruit. People tend to overlook wine from Mexico, which is a real shame! The geography, the climate, the vines, the winemakers… everything is there to produce great wine.” —Jill Weber, owner, Jet Wine Bar, Philadelphia

“For an underrated Sauvignon Blanc, look to Styria (Steiermark), Austria — specifically producers under the STK organization. Steep mountain hillsides, high elevation, and 13 hours of direct sun during the growing season create a unique challenge. Without protection, the grapes are prone to sun-burn. Protection here can come in the form of a wide canopy of foliage, leading to more photosynthesis and thus more aromatic ripeness. The wines result in a perfect combination of flavors for any fan of this grape: the aromatic intensity of New Zealand, the tropical richness of California, and the minerality of the Loire. Start with Hannes Sabathi.” —Andrey Ivanov, beverage director, Nisei, San Francisco

“Sandy Cove Sauvignon Blanc from Marlborough, New Zealand is one of my underrated favorites because it is fresh, vibrant, and tropical. It opens with expressive passion fruit, followed by bright citrus and tropical fruit notes. It’s refreshing, easy to drink, and, most importantly, a wonderful pairing with Indian cuisine. It has relatively limited recognition compared with some of the more widely known Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc producers, which makes it an interesting and unexpected choice for a wine list.” —Prrateek Chaudhary, beverage director, Pataaka, Atlanta

“My favorite and most underrated Sauvignon Blanc these days is a beauty from the Cheverny appellation in the Loire Valley: Domaine du Salvard Cheverny Blanc, imported by Kermit Lynch. It offers crisp lemon and valencia orange notes with a beautiful mid-palate because of the addition of 25 percent Chardonnay, with a lemongrass and savory thyme finish… yummy!” —Thomas Price, master sommelier, 1856 – Culinary Residence, Auburn

“In my estimation, most Sauvignon Blanc is overrated, and Sancerre mania has made the appellation’s name a substitute for exercising any real discernment among its wines. But if pressed, I’d point you toward Hippolyte Reverdy, a family domaine whose Sancerre gives you something to appreciate beyond name recognition and ease of pronunciation. It’s bright and floral, with citrus, a stony finish, and enough texture from a short spell on the lees to smooth out its texture. Drink it with oysters, fresh goat cheese, or a simple green salad.” —Bodhi Landa, sommelier-at-large, Bar Etienne, New York City

“The Quincy region in Loire Valley is an expression not nearly enough people are talking about. While Sancerre gets most of the attention, Quincy was actually one of the first French appellations to receive AOC status. It offers many of the same qualities found in higher-priced Sancerre and Pouilly-Fumé, with vibrant citrus, minerality, and a crisp, refreshing finish.” —Brianna Ellis, general manager, Tannin Bar, Park City, Utah

“Pepper Bridge Winery makes a Sauvignon Blanc that deserves far more attention than it gets. It is new on my list and becoming a staff pick! It balances bright citrus and crisp acidity beautifully, while offering enough texture and subtle richness to make it work at our table. For me, it’s a great example of how the Pacific Northwest can produce Sauvignon Blanc with both freshness and depth.” —Owen Perry, wine director, Lansdowne, Portland

“For me, Sauvignon Blanc from Elgin, South Africa deserves far more recognition for its balance of aromatic intensity and restraint. The region’s cool climate lends freshness and precision to the finest examples, where vivid citrus fruit, vibrant acidity, and subtle flinty notes bring both energy and depth. Paul Clüver Sauvignon Blanc 2025 is a compelling introduction, combining gooseberry, passion fruit, and fresh herbal notes with a saline edge and a textured palate. A small proportion of Sémillon adds fullness while preserving freshness, making it a beautiful companion to seafood.” —Cornelia Duchessa, wine director, BRASS, NYC

“One of the most underrated Sauvignon Blancs is without question from Menetou-Salon in the Loire Valley, just outside of the wildly popular appellation of Sancerre. The wines, specifically from Paul-Henry Pellé in the village of Morogues, come from soils rich in Kimmeridgian limestone and are some of the most nuanced Sauvignons out there. The specific bottle I love is the Pellé’s Menetou-Salon ‘Morogues Blanchais’ 2023.” —Francesco Grosso, wine director, Ai Fiori, NYC

“In a world where the biggest argument is whether New Zealand Sauvignon Blanc, with its grassy and gooseberry flavors, or California’s expression, offering notes of peach and tropical fruit, is the most sought after, it’s easy to overlook some of the original Sauvignon Blancs from France’s Loire Valley. These wines bring a strong minerality and vibrant notes of citrus, particularly lime and lemon.They are a magical pairing with seafood dishes, especially those finished with a squeeze of lemon. They are also incredible alongside fatty dishes, such as duck breast or creamy sauces, where their high acidity balances the richness. Domaine Durand Sancerre is a perfect example of how beautifully this style can shine.” —Lee Nevarez, sommelier, The National, Autograph Collection, Oklahoma City

content:
Bordeaux put the idea of fine wine on the map. The 1855 Classification became a model for identifying quality wines and producers, a concept copied throughout the region, as well as the world over.

But anyone who’s been to Bordeaux knows that those Classified Growths don’t reflect how dynamic and forward-thinking Bordeaux is today. The vast region is populated with family-run estates, organic growers, and new generations eager to put their stamp on a style. And while a changing climate and society have given Bordeaux hard knocks, the sensational headlines don’t fully reflect what’s really going on in a legacy region that’s entering its next chapter.

For those interested in getting to know the modern Bordeaux landscape, we compiled a list of producers showcasing what the region has to offer right now. From historic châteaux ranked in the region’s highest classifications to experimental producers working with amphora aging, here are eight producers to know to get into Bordeaux.

Château Troplong Mondot

Founded in 1700, Troplong Mondot is ranked Premier Grand Cru Classé in the St. Émilion Classification, which was established in 1955. Being located on the Right Bank, Merlot dominates the cuvées, with a touch of Cabernet Sauvignon and Cabernet Franc rounding out the style. Sustainability is the keyword for this St. Émilion estate. The B Corp-certified winery pledges to cut carbon emissions in half by 2030, reaching net zero by 2050. The Grand Vin ranges in price depending on vintage, anywhere from $120 upwards, but like most Bordeaux châteaux, it offers an affordable second label, Mondot.

Château Malartic-Lagravière

Located in Pessac-Léognan, Malartic-Lagravière was one of six estates to be classified for both its red and white wines in the 1953 Graves Classification. Gravel, shell limestone, and clay define the soils. Cabernet Sauvignon dominates the red wines, with Cabernet Franc and Merlot completing the blend. Out of the 180 acres of vineyards, 17 acres are dedicated to Sauvignon Blanc and Semillon. The white wines, such as the flagship Malartic-Lagraviére Blanc, retailing at around $90 are some of the most exciting in all of Bordeaux, with lots of bright acidity and lifted aromatics.

Château Durfort-Vivens

Durfort-Vivens may be a Second Growth in the 1855 Classification, but the Margaux estate is one of the most innovative operators in Bordeaux today. Instead of oak, owners Gonzague and Claire Lurton only use amphoras in the cellar, which they believe brings out the best expression of their Cabernet-focused wines. While Bordeaux is best known for blending different parcels, the couple experiments with single-vineyard expressions. In addition to their Bordeaux property, they own Acaibo winery in Sonoma, bringing another dimension to their knowledge of Cabernet.

Château Pontet-Canet

Pontet-Canet, in the Pauillac appellation, is a leader in biodynamic viticulture. Originally founded in 1781, the Fifth Growth château was purchased by the Tesseron family in 1975. In the 1990s, they converted to biodynamics, a rarity in the region, and paved the way for other estates. In 2015, Justine Tesseron took over, in partnership with her brother, Noé, and their cousins. The family also owns the Napa estate Pym-Rae, which was the former home of actor Robin Williams. There, they continue their biodynamic farming principles and focus on Cabernet-based wines.

Château Lagrange

This St. Julien Third Growth estate prides itself on its 265-acre contiguous vineyard in the appellation’s gravelly soils. Founded in the 1700s, it counts Thomas Jefferson among its celebrity clients. It enjoyed a reputation as a fine wine producer until the late 1800s, when phylloxera, world wars, and other hardships decimated the property. In 1983, Keizo Saji from the Suntory family purchased Lagrange and invested heavily in restorations, notably subdividing the vineyard into 103 plots and taking a detailed approach to grape cultivation. The château produces three red wines at various price points, along with two whites, making this an ideal estate to get into Bordeaux.

Château Haut-Brion

One of the original First Growths in the 1855 Classification, Haut-Brion is one of the most well-known and collected Bordeaux wines. (If opportunity presents itself, it’s worth getting to know all of the First Growths, but Haut-Brion has a fun story to get into.) The reds are led by Cabernet Sauvignon, with Merlot and Cabernet Franc also in the composition. The white wine, a blend of Sauvignon Blanc and Semillon, is an IYKYK wine. Overseeing Haut-Brion and its parent company, Domaine Clarence Dillon, is Prince Robert of Luxembourg, who, before taking over the family estate, worked as a screenwriter in Los Angeles. He wants to bring new drinkers into the Bordeaux fold and, 20 years ago, created the Clarendelle wines, an affordable, lifestyle-driven line. While a bottle of Haut-Brion Grand Vin red might go for $450-plus depending on the vintage, drinkers looking for an entry point to these storied wines can find the Clarendelle for $23.

Château Angélus

Merlot dominates many of the wines in the Right Bank, but Château Angelus in St. Émilion puts Cabernet Franc front and center. The vineyard, a south-facing amphitheater, contains sandy-limestone soils at lower elevations, which is ideal for Cab Franc, while Merlot vines thrive in the heavier clay soils up-slope. Earlier this year, the estate unveiled a new wine cellar, which took 14 years to construct. If the Grand Vin, which can go for $400 or more depending on vintage, is out of budget, the estate also produces second and third labels for a more affordable taste. The second wine, Le Carillon de Angelus, retails for an average of $150, and the third wine, No. 3 d’Angelus, is priced at approximately $60.

Château d’Yquem

Red and white wines are only part of the story; Bordeaux is also the home of Sauternes, one of the most famous sweet wines in the world. In order to create these dessert sips, vintners rely on botrytis, or noble rot, to concentrate sugars in the grapes. Long considered the pinnacle of Sauternes producer, Château d’Yquem’s laborious process requires a careful selection of grapes during harvest, as they believe various levels of botrytis create the ultimate expression of Sauternes. The estate has been certified organic since 2022, which is no small feat considering the same humidity needed for botrytis development challenges general viticulture, with its heightened risk of bad rot. While even half-bottles can retail for $300, it’s worth the investment to understand the art and science of botrytized wines.

content:
Before presenting the final drink of the “Omacocktail,” an omakase-style cocktail tasting at Ophelia in midtown Manhattan, the bartender anoints your frothy coupe with three drops of Louis XIII Cognac. A server swoops in behind with a bump of caviar on an ice tray to pair with the drink, which the bartender also baptizes with droplets of the rare Cognac. The menu describes the drink as a “Japanese-inspired sidecar,” but little else about the Omacocktail experience feels very Japanese.

The 90-minute tasting, which features seven petite cocktails and a smattering of small bites sold through reservation platform Bucket Listers for around $100, is almost uncomfortably Instagrammable — drinks are smoked, atomized, clarified, and even dosed with edible glitter. The theatricality of the whole affair makes the Omacocktail feel more spiritually aligned with Benihana than with the sushi counter at Nobu. “Everyone wants to know what’s going on behind the scenes these days,” says Amir Babayoff, Ophelia’s beverage director. “When you do the Omacocktail, you get to sit with the bartender, and you get to learn about the processes and techniques. It’s very intimate.”

These days, the word omakase is being co-opted to describe all manners of gastronomic experiences. Pujol in Mexico City offers a taco omakase; Pasquale Jones in New York serves pizza omakase; Equipment Room, a listening bar in Austin, curates a vinyl omakase. Cocktail tasting menus are still a rarity, but the word omakase has quietly wormed its way into the vernacular in recent years as top bars look for inventive ways to showcase technique and lure younger drinkers with more mindful bar experiences. The result is a new wave of omakase bars that seek to elevate craft cocktails through guided liquid degustations.

Critics malign the trend as gimmickry; truthers see potential in providing a larger canvas for mixologists to express their artistry. But how much demand there is for these immersive, omakase-inspired cocktail tastings remains unclear.

Understanding the History of Omakase

The roots of omakase can be traced back to street food stalls during Japan’s Edo period between 1603 and 1868. The tradition began as a humble way for busy workers to enjoy seasonal raw fish, fresh from the docks. These early sushi stalls would offer “omakase,” which translated meant: “I leave it to you.” It was customary to trust the vendor to choose the freshest selection of fish. In the late 1990s, omakase emerged as a buzzword for high-end sushi experiences, beginning in Japan and spreading worldwide with influential restaurants like Sukiyabashi Jiro in Tokyo and Nobu in New York City. Today, sushi omakases have become ubiquitous, ranging from exclusive multi-course menus that cost in the thousands to more approachable neighborhood sushi counters.

Some argue that co-opting the word omakase for cocktails obscures the true meaning of the word and undermines its history. “Personally, I don’t think every cocktail tasting menu should be called omakase,” says Shinya Yamao, beverage director of Don’t Be Shy in NYC’s Hudson Square. “A tasting menu describes the format, while omakase describes the relationship between the guest and the person creating the experience. Simply serving a predetermined sequence of cocktails is not enough, in my opinion.”

Others contend that the principles of omakase can be respectfully applied to a bar setting. “To be called an omakase, there should be a focus on technique, seasonality of ingredients, and hospitality,” says Hiro Nishida, founder of Plus Being NYC, a New York-based hospitality consultant that specializes in restaurant development. “To me, it’s a good thing for consumers to embrace a new and exciting vocabulary for cocktail experiences.”

Taking Guests on a Liquid Journey

When Greg Boehm, founder and CEO of Cocktail Kingdom, opened Cocktail Omakase on NYC’s Lower East Side earlier this year, he sought to design a bar experience that prioritized connection as much as cocktails. “Omakase isn’t just a way we describe the menu, it’s fundamental to how the entire experience is structured,” he says. The bar, a collaboration with Tokyo’s Bar Libre, offers a $55 four-course cocktail tasting menu paired with individual bites that changes every two weeks. “We wanted the philosophy behind omakase to inform the experience rather than to use the word as shorthand for a tasting menu. That interaction is as important to us as what’s in the glass.”

Boehm says the bar’s low-slung design was inspired by a traditional sushi counter; guests are seated directly in front of the bartender and can watch each drink being made, as they would with a sushi chef. “The format gives cocktails room to tell a larger story,” he says. “Instead of one drink standing entirely on its own, we can think about how four drinks build on and contrast with one another, how the accompanying bites fit into that progression and how the experience evolves over the course of an hour.” If guests prefer a more customizable experience, a seven-seat bar hidden in the back, inspired by Tokyo’s micro bars, offers à la carte drinks.

“A tasting menu describes the format, while omakase describes the relationship between the guest and the person creating the experience. Simply serving a predetermined sequence of cocktails is not enough, in my opinion.”

Tiger Sun in Atlanta serves a four-course cocktail omakase paired with food ($95 per person) inside a refurbished vintage tour bus, which it describes as: “Tokyo meets Scorsese in a neon-lit dojo on wheels.” Each new menu is themed around a cult film from the ’70s, ’80s, or ’90s with cocktail recipes inspired by obscure movie references from films like “The Karate Kid” and “Forrest Gump.” A recent “Back to the Future” menu featured a cocktail called the “Flux Capacitor,” made with reposado tequila, Strega, and pineapple-basil cordial garnished with a glow-stick.

“When guests step on the bus, we want them to sit back and relax and enjoy whatever ride we’re taking them on,” beverage director Heather Rule says. “The term omakase lends itself well to that because if you were having a true omakase, you’re trusting the chef and the front-of-house to show you an experience you may not have had otherwise if you were just picking drinks for yourself.”

Riding the Omakase Wave

Even though most of these cocktail tastings have no spiritual connection to Japan, branding them as omakases can be an effective marketing tool. The word carries a certain cachet in the restaurant world, synonymous with luxury. So much so that “bromakases” — as the New York Times referred to the trend of finance bros protein-maxxing in premium sushi restaurants — have replaced trophy steaks as the ultimate status meal. “Calling it an omakase creates an expectation in the guest’s mind that they’re in for something more sophisticated or elevated,” Babayoff says.

Some bars have had to contend with media branding their cocktail tastings as omakases, even when they don’t explicitly use the term on their menus. “We never positioned the experience as an omakase,” says Army Sadeghi, owner of The Arc Room in Houston, a 10-seat bar which offers a five-course cocktail tasting menu with “seasonal bites” for $95. “In the beginning, there was some press where writers applied the term to what we’re doing, but it wasn’t really our intent to brand it that way,” he says. “I just don’t want there to be any confusion. Thankfully, we haven’t had any issues so far with anyone thinking we’re serving sushi.”

“Omakase isn’t just a way we describe the menu, it’s fundamental to how the entire experience is structured.”

With so many different tasting experiences being marketed as omakases nowadays, Nishida says the market has reached a saturation point. “In the culinary world, there is already a next generation of Japanese buzz words like kaiseki and kappo because customers are getting exhausted with everything being called an omakase.”

But Rule believes that consumers are still seeking out programmed experiences like the one at Tiger Sun to mitigate decision fatigue. “After Covid, I think people came back into the world exhausted and overwhelmed by so many choices,” she says. “People started to really consider how they’re spending their money when they go out to eat or drink. I think that’s why these kinds of immersive experiences resonate with people.”

Will Cocktail Omakases Last?

Not everyone is convinced that the omakase trend in bars has legs. Skeptics question whether these experiences are worthy of the care and craft that go into a true omakase. “With a real omakase, you trust the sushi chef because he’s trained on how to make rice for 30 years before he was even allowed to touch fish,” says Sarah Morrissey, beverage director for Golden Age Hospitality and VinePair contributor. “But if calling something a cocktail omakase is just an excuse to put a green drink on the menu with 17 different ingredients so influencers can make content, I’m not in favor of it. I don’t need a one-ounce rotisserie chicken Martini course.”

Jonathan Adler, former Shinji’s beverage director and a partner in the forthcoming Bar Chiqui in New York’s Greenwich Village, has doubts that the cocktail omakase trend will last because the addressable market is so small. “Compared to people who go out for restaurant tasting menus, the clientele who wants this kind of omakase bar experience is even more niche,” he says. Static menus are also less attractive for repeat customers, who may feel like visiting these omakase bars to experience them once is sufficient — a tenuous model for longevity.

Yamao cites Gen Yamamoto’s eponymous bar in Tokyo, which opened in 2013, as the model for omakase’s staying power in bars. But he stresses that the seasonality of Yamamoto’s menu and how he customizes the experience for each guest is the key to its lasting success. Adler points to more recent examples like Esencia at Sips in Barcelona and Cariño at Handshake in Mexico City as evidence of the genre’s potential. But he’s still skeptical that the market will support more of these omakase-style concepts. “I don’t think this will be a long-term trend,” he says. “It’s become an exercise in ego-driven creativity more than anything.”

content:
The American craft beer industry continued to struggle in 2025. The net number of craft breweries contracted for the second year in a row, and the sector’s total production dipped by 4 percent year-over-year. But some reports suggest that hope for recovery is on the horizon: The sector’s market share by volume inched upward — albeit by 0.2 percent — from the previous year’s figures.

Despite these challenges, the roughly 9,700 breweries around the country continue to churn out fan-favorite brews. To see which beer is the most beloved in each state and Washington, D.C., we consulted Beer Advocate’s list of the top-rated beers around the country. As a baseline, only beers with over 100 ratings on the platform were considered for this list.

India Pale Ales and stouts tied for the most-favored beer styles, claiming 20 states each. The two categories maintained their strongholds, as they were the two top performing styles on last year’s list. And within each, there were some clear favorite sub-categories, from the juicy, quaffable hazy IPAs to the rich, dessert-like pastry stouts. Young Jr. filed last Friday. Viewers likewise gulped in second-hand embarrassment, prompting a wave of memes and roasts to swarm social media platforms.

Some of the wines swiped included Antinori’s Guada al Tasso and Solaia expressions, which are among the region’s most prized bottlings. A group of up to 10 men allegedly disabled the property’s security alarms and, according to security footage, loaded the thousands of bottles into two trucks before driving off — all within a span of three hours.

content:
In 2020, Lois and Dave Cho became the first Korean American winemakers in Oregon when they launched CHO Wines in the Willamette Valley. The fast-growing winery quickly amassed a following and received critical acclaim, but they kept fielding the same question: “What informs your palate for wine?”

The answer to that question grew to become so much more than they expected. The two kept thinking back to the Korean food they enjoyed as children, saying that they ultimately hoped for the bottles from CHO Wines to complement their heritage’s cuisine. But pondering their response revealed a more sobering reality: The Asian-American wine scene is far less appreciated than its culinary counterpart.

Considering their wine as something to be paired with Korean food sparked the idea of hosting a potluck for AAPI folks around the Willamette Valley. The brainstorming snowballed from there, and turned into a full-blown festival. In hopes of placing Asian American–made wine on the same level as food, the Chos officially launched AAPI Food & Wine in 2023.

“The first year, we hosted 12 Portland chefs and five Asian American Pacific Islander-owned wineries from the Willamette Valley,” Lois Cho says. “We had 1,000 people show up, and it was sold out.”

Though it came together in a matter of weeks, the inaugural event’s response was sentimental. “Multiple people came up to me with tears in their eyes,” Lois says. “I knew it was going to be a kick-ass party, but I didn’t realize that it was going to be so emotional.”

That emotional response was proof of concept. Since its debut, AAPI Food & Wine has held three annual walkaround festivals in Oregon, inviting participants to set up stalls with samples for attendees to learn and taste. Earlier this year, it inaugurated its expansion to the East Coast with a three-day-long celebration in New York City. Each of the events has been a near or total sell-out. Now, a group of board members handle the nonprofit’s operations, including secretary and volunteer director Sylvia Choi and vendor relations and events director Jane Barmore.

In the U.S., AAPI communities have been taught to assimilate to American culture and keep quiet to avoid scrutiny, Lois says. But after generations of repression, an outward embrace of Asian American food and wine was cause for celebration.

“A lot of our history has been about flying under the radar and not making a fuss,” she says. “This new generation is now really coming more into the spotlight and saying, ‘This is our heritage, and this is how it plays into food and wine.’”

The first Oregon festival featured beloved wineries like Hundred Suns Wine and Et Fille Wines, as well as Portland-based restaurants like Sun Rice and Matta. The nonprofit has since grown to amass a roster of other well-regarded chefs, winemakers, and collaborators, hosting events with industry pros like winemaker Sashi Moorman of Evening Land Vineyards and James Beard Award-winning bakers Jin Caldwell and Kyurim “Q” Lee of JinJu Patisserie. During its NYC residency this March, AAPI Food & Wine partnered with Atoboy, a Korean restaurant among the city’s culinary elite. With big-name affiliations and one expansion already under its belt, the nonprofit is ready for more growth.

“We’re already in chats about doing events in Los Angeles, Seattle, Chicago, D.C., and hopefully Austin at some point,” Lois says. “We keep getting the requests.”

Lois hopes to highlight chefs and winemakers outside of the Pacific Northwest and New York metropolitan areas with these expansions. After focusing on well-known chefs at previous festivals, she wants to include up-and-coming cooks who operate small brick-and-mortars or food carts.

And as the culinary scene increasingly celebrates AAPI cuisine, Lois sees that the wine industry is beginning to catch on. Some of the most celebrated sommeliers and beverage directors of today are AAPI-identifying, leading a pack of others to follow suit.

“There are a bunch of newcomers who are sharing their experiences getting into wine and pursuing their Master Sommelier certification,” she says.

Just as the first festival grew from a potluck, AAPI Food & Wine has expanded beyond anything Lois imagined. The community of participants, partners, and attendees the festival has corralled is the biggest driver in fueling its momentum, she says.

“Now, it’s like people don’t even know we’re involved in it,” she says. “They’re just like, ‘Oh my gosh, have you heard of AAPI Food & Wine? I’m like, ‘Yeah, my husband and I actually started it.’”

content:
Kimball House stands in a former train depot in the Atlanta suburb of Decatur, Ga. It gets its name from a historic Atlanta hotel. Its moniker was chosen to honor the long-gone hotel bars that drove the city’s cocktail culture at the turn of the 20th century.

These elements help Kimball House share the history and traditions of a city which tend to gravitate toward contemporary design and aesthetic. Yet they’re not what make Kimball House such an enduring Atlanta institution. Rather, they are meant to be respectfully referential anecdotes for a space that began carving its own distinctive character from the moment it opened in 2013.

“When we opened, we wanted to make sure we were doing an homage without making it an amusement park,” explains Kimball House co-founder and beverage director Miles Macquarrie. “We also saw that so much of Atlanta had modern polish, and we knew we didn’t want that.”

The secret sauce allowing Kimball House to be a seamless portal linking past and present is its insistence to engage in honest hospitality. This is different from Southern hospitality, which can oftentimes be reduced to a cliched trope punctuated by y’alls and drawls. It’s a warm, familial form of service that’s meticulous in its execution but relaxed in its presentation, set in an environment that doesn’t take itself too seriously — it’s hard to be stuffy when there’s a taxidermied bobcat overlooking the space from a cozy nook. This formula shields their critically-acclaimed food menu from pretension, regardless of the dish’s ambitiousness.

While guests can feast on expected fare like sliced ribeye and oysters without feeling too fancy, they can also opt to dig into elevated dishes with distinctive regional elements to provide a touch of homespun flair, like trout with blue corn grits and okra or pork loin accompanied by green tomatoes and peaches. Kimball House’s must-have buttery Hawaiian rolls with peach preserves set a chic-yet-relaxed tone at the meal’s outset, regardless of the culinary direction the night takes.

Macquarrie’s bar program also provides a clean snapshot of this philosophy. The menu’s drinks draw equal inspiration from classic precision-driven techniques and modern technological innovation, underscored by a culinary approach accentuated by fresh ingredients grown in their on-site garden. This produces plenty of delicious, nerdy cocktails like a Fig & Honey Sour or a Cognac-based, force-carbonated take on the classic French 75.

“We use modern techniques, but we won’t mention them on the menu,” Macquarrie says. “To us, those techniques are just a component of a great drink.”

Kimball House’s glassware furthers such modesty. The venue presents drinks in a mismatched assortment of vintage vessels they’ve amassed through years of scouring Atlanta’s robust antique scene. The collection naturally plays into Kimball House’s easygoing homespun vibe, but it also allows the venue another avenue to connect with Atlanta’s past in a more intimate fashion.

“The glasses make you think of history. It may make you think what people were drinking in those glasses 30 or 40 years ago, or even longer,” Macquarrie says. “There’s a story in every glass, and using them shows that we care enough to share those stories.”

Such thoughtfulness is truly indicative of Kimball House’s devotion to honest hospitality, and this adherence fuels their iconic status. It also puts them in a position to help draw national attention to Atlanta and a cocktail scene that flies so under the radar, it’s practically subterranean. According to Macquarrie, any added attention is a bonus that supplements their main focus.

“Atlanta always takes a back seat to cities like New York and San Francisco,” he says. “I don’t know why, but that’s fine. After all these years, we still just want to run a good restaurant.”

content:
In the whiskey world, if you’re doing everything yourself — if you’re not cutting any corners, if you’re trying to be a true original — it can take quite a while, perhaps even more than a full decade to become “up-and-coming.”

Such is the case with Still Austin Whiskey Co.

“It takes time. It does take time,” says Chris Seals, the CEO at Still Austin. “But it’s not just waiting around. Like, this is probably the most dynamic time in our lives, 15 years in.”

For Still Austin, it would take a retirement, state laws to be changed, a new sub-category to emerge, and we haven’t even got to all the toil of assembling a team, sourcing grains, fermenting, distilling, aging, bottling, and packaging.

It was back in 2012 when Cleveland Seals began looking for a retirement project and, hey, wouldn’t opening a whiskey distillery be fun? By that year, American whiskey was still in the early stages of explosive growth, going from 190 proof gallons produced in 2012 to well over 350 million by 2024 according to the TTB. Cleveland asked his son, Chris — who was working as an economist and risk manager at the time, perhaps aptly for this crazy endeavor — to join him. Chris thought success was unlikely and the time commitment would be immense, but at least the time would be spent with his dad, who he had struggled to forge a relationship with after coming out in his 20s.

Chris Seals wanted to live life as his true self and wanted to create a whiskey brand based on those values.

“You can’t be your true self when you fake it,” he says. “You have to let people see who you truly are and like that.”

That time with his father would initially start with research — traveling the country trying whiskeys. It was still quite difficult to start a distillery in Texas, until a 2013 law would allow for in-state distillers to sell their spirits directly to consumers as well as offer on-premise tastings.

By 2014, the Seals, along with their partners Andrew and Lisa Braunberg and Sal and Joanna Salinas, had broken ground on a facility in the St. Elmo neighborhood Austin. By 2017, head distiller John Schrepel, who had formerly run operations at New York’s Black Dirt Distillery, had distilled their first liquid using his own unique mashbills. Industry legend Nancy Fraley would advise on the maturation and blending using her signature élevage methods to help them in their grain-to-glass journey.

Yet even from the get-go, it was never solely about the liquid.

“There’s four things that we really want to give people,” says Seals. “We want them to feel deeply human. We want them to feel seen. We want them to feel free to express themselves. And we want them to feel the confidence to be distinct. If you can press those four, you are authentic.”

Still Austin would do this by focusing more on the people — their employees, their co-workers, their fellow artists, their customers — than on the liquid. The bottles have stunning, full-color labels painted by Texas artist Marc Burckhardt. Each label is meant to capture and honor the unique people that live among them in the so-called “Live Music Capital of the World,” whether artists, musicians, or naturalists. Seals has long aspired to use his burgeoning brand to create a new mythology for the creatives in the Austin community. He wanted to inspire these people whether they gave a damn about whiskey or not.

But that’s not to say that the whiskey isn’t stellar.

And this is pure Texas whiskey to be clear. It’s made from 100 percent Texas grains grown by Texas farmers and turned into Texas distillate aged in the unique climate of the hot and often erratic Texas Hill Country.

The Musician, Still Austin’s straight bourbon whiskey, uses the same chef-grade white corn that the area’s famous tortilla makers do. The result is a bourbon with a sort of a tropical piña colada note on the nose and palate of rich toffee and brown butter.

The Artist, their straight rye whiskey, employs a mashbill of 100 percent Brasetto rye, creating something wholly unique from the 95/5 rye you might be used to — theirs is like a chocolate-dipped cherry backed by nutmeg, clove, and a spicy cinnamon.

“There’s something special that goes on in our brains when we encounter something that astonishes us,” says Seals. “When the creativity is shocking, it releases a cocktail of hormones that induces wanting. One of the strongest triggers of that is individuality, novelty, and astonishment.” At Still Austin, they do that through flavor and with their one-of-a-kind painted label packaging. “And we do that with how we show up.”

Customers are showing up too. Last year saw some 100,000 visitors to the distillery. They come to hang with friends, to be a part of this unique community, to perhaps listen to live music on The Antone’s Stage at Still Austin. But the brand has also attracted fans from the connoisseurial community at large, who chase yearly one-offs like their Blue and Red Corn Bourbons and trade online for special single barrels, especially ones labeled “Nancy’s Pick.”

“That authenticity, it’s actually hard to do,” says Seals. “I think part of the reason that this award means so much to me right now is the things that we strive for now are much more human than they are simply a whiskey product.”

title: Art and Wine Have a Long History. But Does Art Sell Wine?
summary:
Increasingly, a bottle of wine these days seems to arrive with an artist attached; on a label, via a vineyard commission, through social media scrolls. The rationale for these arty collaborations is by now well-rehearsed: to attract new audiences, differentiate a brand, and increase cultural capital. ”Art enables us to connect with a cultured audience, and is also a good way to keep your brand alive,” says Fabien Vallérian, the international director of arts and culture at Ruinart, which has ostensibly been at it since 1896, when Alphonse Mucha, an Art Nouveau artist, designed the first ad for the Maison.

content:
Increasingly, a bottle of wine these days seems to arrive with an artist attached; on a label, via a vineyard commission, through social media scrolls. The rationale for these arty collaborations is by now well-rehearsed: to attract new audiences, differentiate a brand, and increase cultural capital.

“Art enables us to connect with a cultured audience, and is also a good way to keep your brand alive,” says Fabien Vallérian, the international director of arts and culture at Ruinart, which has ostensibly been at it since 1896, when Alphonse Mucha, an Art Nouveau artist, designed the first ad for the Maison. Against shifting drinking habits and crowded shelf space, linking wine to art can signal higher value, create buzz, and lend innovation credentials to a brand.

The question is whether it works for the everyday wine brands themselves, whether it serves smaller scale producers running on tight margins, and whether audiences who pay for art and cultural access in other contexts value wine the same way.

The empirical basis is thin. Research into arts sponsorship finds plenty of potential for goodwill and engagement (who doesn’t like the thrill of opening the post-launch party goodie bag in the cab home?), but less evidence of what happens at the till. Consumer studies can show an “art infusion” effect, in which visual art can raise perceived value and luxury associations, while eye-tracking studies of wine labels have found pictorial elements attract the most attention, and label attractiveness predicts willingness to pay. But the effect varies by artwork, product, and consumer, and brands themselves rarely publish controlled sales data capable of proving a return.

Impecunious arts organizations expect product donations from wine brands, which suggests a shaky grasp of the latter’s balance sheet. Wine is capital-intensive business with tight, often impossible margins, few brands can afford to bankroll another “collab” and hope some cultural capital sticks, so it’s worth separating the various forms the wine-art relationship takes in the market today, and asking what each is actually for.

The Prestige Exception: When the Bottle Becomes the Object

The art-plus-wine model has been propelled by blue-chip Champagne brands over the past three decades, where the boundary between wine and art object blurs. Since the 2006 vintage, Louis Roederer has collaborated with French designer Philippe Starck on its zero-dosage Brut Nature, a project Starck accepted only once he could have input into the cuvée itself. Dom Pérignon‘s collaborations with world-renowned and commercially successful artists include Jeff Koons’ 2013 Balloon Venus, built around Rose Vintage 2003; labels for Vintage 2015 using Jean-Michel Basquiat’s “In Italian” (Basquiat died in 1988); and Takashi Murakami’s designs for Vintage 2015 and the first Rosé Vintage 2010. Veuve Clicquot handed the design of La Grande Dame 2012 to Yayoi Kusama.

Such limited editions, launches, and their relaunches keep these brands in conversation and turn the wine and especially its packaging into sought-after objects for collectors more than drinkers — Kusama’s numbered sculpture 71/100, complete with a bottle of La Grande Dame 2012, sold at auction for £87,720 in January. But prestige editions reveal little about whether art sells ordinary wine in ordinary quantities.

Back in the still wine aisles, rarely does a season pass without a wine “doing art,” partnering at a gallery launch, or doing a restaurant activation tie-in. There are charitable one-offs, a separate economy from selling wine: in 2013 a nine-litre Salmanazar of Ornellaia 2010, customized by Michelangelo Pistoletto, sold for £80,000 at Sotheby’s, then the highest price paid at auction for a single bottle of Italian wine.

“The wine was first and the fact of doing things differently than things had been done before was first. And then art came to partner on this adventure.”

At the everyday end, Campo Viejo has put street artists including Okuda San Miguel and Remed on supermarket-priced Riojas, with Pernod Ricard citing distinctive packaging among drivers of growth to a record three million cases annually by 2020; Prophecy Wines built its core range around Victo Ngai’s tarot-like illustrations; while Ecco Domani, Santero, and even Aldi have used artist or designer labels to distinguish their bottles.

The Label: What It Can and Cannot Do

The artist label is the most established form of partnership. It is most convincing when a genuine bond joins winery and artist, a shared philosophy legible in both bottle and image. Without it, the strategy reads as a marketing ploy rather than a statement and loses both audiences at once. Its lineage traces to Château Mouton Rothschild, where in 1924 Baron Philippe commissioned Jean Carlu, a graphic designer, to reinterpret the family crest for his first vintage label. The gesture celebrated the mise en bouteille au château milestone, as much as aesthetics, a signal of radical innovation in the industry, like an avant-garde manifesto.

“The wine was first and the fact of doing things differently than things had been done before was first. And then art came to partner on this adventure,” says Julien de Beaumarchais de Rothschild, co-owner of Château Mouton Rothschild, who oversees the estate’s relationship with artists. The labels have become a roll-call of the most commercially significant 20th-century artists since Braque created the label for the 1955 vintage. Dalí followed in 1958, Picasso’s estate for the 1973 release (posthumously to mark promotion to first growth), Warhol designed 1975 vintage label; canonical now, but each in their own time matched the estate’s spirit of disruption and innovation.

Here is the inconvenient finding. Across 52 post-reveal reviews covering the past 12 vintages of Chateau Mouton’s grand vin, only seven named the artist, two described the artwork and none incorporated it into the wine’s score or qualitative judgement. This might suggest the trade and wine nerds treat the artist as paratext, just promotional material outside the serious evaluation of the wine. That approach misses what an Olafur Eliasson (2019) or an Anish Kapoor (2009) is signalling on a Mouton artist label: a form of translation, giving voice to a year or a region, making visible the most immaterial things a wine can hold: transmitting terroir.

This is why the label works hardest when producer and artist share a cause. In 2009, South Africa’s revered winemaker, Eben Sadie, made six wines from old vines, released as a series of 280 boxed sets, with ink-wash drawings and collages inspired by their West Coast vineyards drawn by its most important artist, William Kentridge, a known oenophile. “It wasn’t about business — at no point money was exchanged,” Sadie says. “It was about putting something out there to say, here’s part of our history in wine,” a history in wine and art that had been once overlooked by both wine and art markets.

At the other end sit intimate stories, almost inside jokes between wineries and artists captured on a label design. Leeuwin Estate’s Art Series has featured Australian artists since its first vintage in 1980, with each label carrying its own anecdote — from a better deal on a John Kelly than the National Gallery managed, to keeping all four of John Olsen’s frog drawings for its Riesling, to co-founder Tricia Horgan continuing to scout artists for the collection (“I’ve got my eye on you,” she tells them). Gut Oggau’s bottles each carry the face of an invented family member drawn by Jung von Matt, ageing a little with every vintage. Cult wines such as Montevertine’s Le Pergole Torte continue to feature vintage labels illustrated with the elegant mystery women drawn by Alberto Manfredi, even after his passing.

The Estate As Gallery

A different kind of partnership forms through oenotourism, with sculpture parks and gallery spaces drawing visitors to the other side of the bottle. Italy is exemplary: around 60 wine-producing sites exist, according to the University of Verona. These are heirs to a tradition of placing contemporary art in rural spaces that runs back to the 1960s. The Ceretto estate in Piedmont reports its Sol LeWitt and David Tremlett designed Barolo Chapel draws at least 30,000 visitors a year, and at least another 10,000 visiting the winery. From Ca’ del Bosco, to Castello di Ama, to Feudi di San Gregorio, to Vini Planeta, tastings unfold among commissions and collections.

Here, art plausibly does sell wine through the captive audience and experiential pleasure of drinking wine where it is made. But the more compelling examples involve skin in the game: owners committing personal capital, land, and years to cultural projects that become part of the foundation rather than an annual marketing line. Places like Bodega Colomé where Donald Hess planted a museum devoted to James Turrell 2,300 metres up in the Andes. Or David Walsh blasting and burrowing his subterranean Museum of Old and New Art (MONA) three levels into the sandstone beneath Moorilla’s historic Pinot Noir vineyard on Hobart’s Berriedale Peninsula in Tasmania. The commercial logic of bringing people physically onto a wine estate is clearer more generally. Wine Australia found 66.7 percent of cellar-door visitors bought wine during their visit, averaging 4.42 bottles, while follow-up research found a 16 percent net gain in buyers among those who’d never previously bought a brand.

“We believe artists are the best ambassadors to raise awareness about ecology. You’re not just there to drink Champagne, you’re also there to think about protecting the planet.”

Château La Coste in Provence is an exemplary case: since it opened in 2011, art has been continuously integrated into the landscape, with sculptures and pavilions by Tadao Ando, Frank Gehry, and Tracey Emin making the domain a cultural destination in its own right. Official tourism figures recorded 200,000 visitors in 2017, rising to a reported 400,000 annually in 2024. The estate’s development director, Jérôme Scheher, says 25 percent of its 700,000 bottles are sold directly onsite.

Owner Paddy McKillen’s friendships with the architects and artists make the results organic. In June, the estate released Madame ‘B’, a rosé from the 2025 vintage, in an inaugural run of 10,000 bottles carrying a butterfly design by Damien Hirst continuing a long-standing friendship between the pair and of Hirst’s 2024 estate-wide exhibition, “The Light That Shines.” “The château is a place we both love and from which we draw inspiration,” McKillen says. The continuing build-out, including a wine school and more cellar space, puts the cultural project into the winery’s long-term development rather than an annual activation budget.

You Are Cordially Invited: The Art x Wine Event

Commissions and sponsorship can tie a wine to a cultural moment, borrowing audiences and associations that conventional advertising struggles to reach. England’s burgeoning wine industry is a revealing case. In its 2025 Industry Report, WineGB has sales up 200 percent between 2018 and 2024, reaching 9.1 million bottles, while producers have become increasingly culturally acquisitive. Artelium Wine Estate commissions artists across labels and exhibitions; Balfour Winery commissioned artists to interpret its limited Winemakers’ Collection; Nyetimber is taking the Ruinart route, attaching English sparkling wine to sponsorship of cultural institutions from the National Gallery to the V&A and Design Museum. Vines take years to mature; cultural capital can be acquired rather faster. Getting the art world to drink your wine for free is one thing; getting it to pay for the next bottle is another.

Since 2018 the historic Veronese producer Pasqua has invested nearly €6 million in contemporary art encompassing labels, immersive installations, exhibitions, and programs. CEO Riccardo Pasqua says the aim is to reach consumers through “entertainment, beauty, and lifestyle”, opening the winery to spaces once considered “unorthodox.” Its ‘Artistic Projects’ open call this year drew over 200 applications, and selected Sara Ricciardi whose installation appeared at Palazzo Maffei during Vinitaly. Here, the investment is substantial and sustained; the puzzle is still measurement. Exposure, attendance, and engagement can be counted, isolating the arts’s effect on sales is harder. A delighted opening-night audience delighted at the opening is not yet a customer at the till.

The buzz generated by continuous events can also hide the better work. Ruinart excels at presence at the fairs and biennales, the art world guzzling its blanc de blancs, but the glamor obscures a serious arts commissioning program running since 2008, asking artists such as Vik Muniz and David Shrigley to answer questions on climate change, sustainability, and nature, now extended to a younger roster of commissioned artists and designers. “We believe artists are the best ambassadors to raise awareness about ecology,” says Frédéric Dufour, president of Maison Ruinart. As if on cue, the American artist Andrea Bowers, a participant in this Conversations with Nature commission, adds: “You’re not just there to drink Champagne, you’re also there to think about protecting the planet.”

The Verdict: Attention Is Not a Sale

It is a crowded moment for collaborations between almost everything and the art world, and a brand that places an artwork on a bottle and calls the result “art” enters an increasingly skeptical field. The evidence suggests that art can influence how consumers see wine: attracting attention, raising perceived value, making a bottle memorable, and in the right setting, encouraging purchase or visit. What remains harder to prove is whether the artwork itself produces sustained incremental sales rather than a temporary lift in attention or footfall.

That makes the nature of the partnership matter. The strongest partnerships require patience, capital, and commitment beyond an annual campaign; the credible ones feel almost accidental, incidental to what the winery was doing anyway. Mouton’s labels grew from commitment to innovation; La Coste’s commissions from friendship and sustained project pipeline; Ruinart’s core arts engagement from years of investment in a theme. Independent producers, struggling with the usual pressures at the best of times, rarely have that luxury.

As collaborations multiply, consumers have also become more practiced at reading them. Once the museum or gallery moves onto the small space of a label, into an event or across an estate, the artwork and cultural claim are judged alongside the wine. Art can change what a consumer notices and remembers. Whether it changes what they buy depends on more than putting an artist’s name on the bottle.

Though Zinfandel’s rich history reaches back to the vineyards of Croatia, the grape variety has had a massive impact on wine drinking culture in the U.S. Originally brought to California by a Boston ship captain, the Zinfandel grape carried winemakers through the Gold Rush and through the evolution of California wine country. Though Cabernet Sauvignon took over as the variety dominating the conversation around California wine, there are still some producers who embrace Zinfandel as one of the state’s most important grapes.

Because of this history, California boasts a number of hidden pockets of old vine plantings that date back 50 to over 100 years. The wines made from these sites often have the term “old vines” on the label to indicate the grapes were sourced from one of these longstanding plots. On this list, you’ll see families that have been farming this grape for generations, long before Cab was king.

From bottles that showcase Zinfandel’s bold, ripe fruit character to those that feature a more restrained side — plus a few from its original home in Croatia — here are the 30 best Zinfandels to drink in 2026.

Why You Should Trust VinePair

Every year, VinePair conducts dozens of tastings for our “Buy This Booze” product roundups, highlighting the best bottles across the world’s most popular wine and spirits categories.

Within this scope, VinePair’s tasting and editorial staff samples thousands of bottles every year. This ensures we have a close eye on what’s new and exciting. Crucially, it also provides us with the context needed to distinguish the simply good from the truly great, whether from a quality or value-for-money perspective — or both.

Ultimately, our mission is to offer a clear, reliable source of information for drinkers, providing an overview applicable to day-to-day buying and drinking. Learn more about VinePair’s tastings and reviews department here.

How We Taste

We believe in tasting all products as our readers typically would: with full knowledge of the producer and — importantly — price. Our tastings are therefore not conducted blind.

VinePair’s tasting panel evaluates every wine on its aromas, flavors, structure, balance, and quality. We also consider whether or not the wine showed typicity for its specific grape or region.

How We Compiled This List

In order to provide our readers with the most comprehensive and thoroughly tested list of the best Zinfandels to buy, VinePair invited producers, distributors, and PR firms working on their behalf to send samples for consideration. These bottles were submitted free of charge — producers didn’t pay to submit nor did VinePair pay for the products. All were requested with the clear understanding that submission does not guarantee inclusion in the final list.

For the Zinfandel roundup, we assigned a score to each product on a 100-point scale based on the quality and intensity of its aromas, flavors, texture, and finish. Then we reviewed all scores and compiled an editorially driven list that meets our criteria of best Zinfandels to buy right now. Each wine was assessed on quality, price, and availability to compile the final list.

The Best Value Zinfandel

Cline Family Cellars Ancient Vines Zinfandel 2024

This wine comes from a disappearing AVA. Contra Costa Valley is there, but the threat of urban development is real because of its proximity to the San Francisco Bay. For wine historians and preservationists, this land is part of America’s deep wine history. Most of the vines here are 100 to 140 years old, first planted in the mid-19th century. Bottles are on the market right now from vineyards that no longer exist.

Families like the Clines, among others, are trying to keep this vineyard land alive with bottles like the Ancient Vines Zinfandel. It captures the history of how we became a wine-drinking culture and is a worthy purchase to help preserve our viticultural history. The Zin grapes are sourced from a vineyard located on the sandy banks of the Sacramento-San Joaquin River Delta, with some vines reaching well over 100 years old. The result is a wonderfully concentrated wine, with impressively rich character for its under-$25 price point. It has a savory nose with blackberry and tea notes. It also has a hint of aged balsamic and vanilla bean. The palate is delicious and juicy, with soft fruit supported by medium acidity. This is a wine you should buy a lot of and have on hand to impress your friends with awesome American wine.

It is still a big, beautiful, powerful Zin. So this year we’re spotlighting a wine of the same caliber, but a completely different style.

Steve and Jill Matthiasson started Matthiasson Wines in Napa in 2003 with the goal of working with sustainable farming practices to make balanced, refined wines in a region more known for its bold, high-ABV wines. Grapes for this bottling were sourced from Sonoma’s Armor Plate Vineyard, a dry farmed, organic vineyard that was planted in the 1890s. It is a stunning example of Zinfandel, with crushed wild berries and cured black olives flecked with a light dusting of peppercorns. FAQs

Where is Zinfandel from?

Originally, the Zinfandel grape was from the country of Croatia. DNA profiling in the late ‘90s shows that it has the same genetic makeup of the native Tribidrag grape, also known as Crljenak Kaštelanski.

Where is Zinfandel grown?

Zinfandel as we know it grows mostly on the West Coast of the United States. It is mostly concentrated in the Dry Creek AVA and the Lodi AVA, though it is prevalent across Sonoma County. It can also be found in smaller quantities in Oregon and Washington State.

What is old-vine Zinfandel?

There is no official definition for old-vine Zinfandel but it is generally agreed upon that a vine 50 years or older is considered “old” or “ancient.” Some consider 30 years to be enough. Since there are so many historic sites in California, it’s more common to see this designation on Zinfandel bottlings from the state than other grapes.

And between the powerhouse Savvy B-producing region of Marlborough, New Zealand and the always-popular Sancerre, most of that space is dedicated to the heavy-hitting brands and regions. But there are great wines to discover beyond the big names, whether you’re a fan of the grape’s lean, mineral-driven side or the bolder expressions brimming with passion fruit and jalapeño.

It’s easy for wine lovers to gravitate toward an old reliable, but with such a wide variety of expressions, it’s well worth diving into the world of Sauvignon Blanc to uncover its hidden gems. To figure out which bottles deserve a little more love, we asked 10 sommeliers to name the most underrated Sauvignon Blanc on the market right now. From sleeper Loire Valley sub-regions to unsung producers in Austria, here’s what they said.

The most underrated Sauvignon Blanc, according to sommeliers:

  • Casa Jipi Sauvignon Blanc
  • Hannes Sabathi Sauvignon Blanc
  • Sandy Cove Sauvignon Blanc
  • Domaine du Salvard Cheverny Blanc 2024
  • Sancerre Domaine Hippolyte Reverdy 2025
  • Sauvignon Blanc from Quincy
  • Pepper Bridge Winery Sauvignon Blanc
  • Paul Clüver Sauvignon Blanc 2025
  • Domaine Pellé Menetou-Salon Morogues Les Blanchais 2023
  • Domaine Durand Sancerre

“I really like Casa Jipi Sauvignon Blanc from Baja and their awesome winemaker, Lulu Martinez. It is a little fuller — but still fresh and crisp — and has great melon and fresh jalapeño notes. The citrus runs to orange, and it has an amazing salinity that brings a little curd out of the grapefruit. People tend to overlook wine from Mexico, which is a real shame! The geography, the climate, the vines, the winemakers… everything is there to produce great wine.” —Jill Weber, owner, Jet Wine Bar, Philadelphia

“For an underrated Sauvignon Blanc, look to Styria (Steiermark), Austria — specifically producers under the STK organization. Steep mountain hillsides, high elevation, and 13 hours of direct sun during the growing season create a unique challenge. Without protection, the grapes are prone to sun-burn. Protection here can come in the form of a wide canopy of foliage, leading to more photosynthesis and thus more aromatic ripeness. The wines result in a perfect combination of flavors for any fan of this grape: the aromatic intensity of New Zealand, the tropical richness of California, and the minerality of the Loire. Start with Hannes Sabathi.” —Andrey Ivanov, beverage director, Nisei, San Francisco

“Sandy Cove Sauvignon Blanc from Marlborough, New Zealand is one of my underrated favorites because it is fresh, vibrant, and tropical. It opens with expressive passion fruit, followed by bright citrus and tropical fruit notes. It’s refreshing, easy to drink, and, most importantly, a wonderful pairing with Indian cuisine. It has relatively limited recognition compared with some of the more widely known Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc producers, which makes it an interesting and unexpected choice for a wine list.” —Prrateek Chaudhary, beverage director, Pataaka, Atlanta

“My favorite and most underrated Sauvignon Blanc these days is a beauty from the Cheverny appellation in the Loire Valley: Domaine du Salvard Cheverny Blanc, imported by Kermit Lynch. It offers crisp lemon and valencia orange notes with a beautiful mid-palate because of the addition of 25 percent Chardonnay, with a lemongrass and savory thyme finish… yummy!” —Thomas Price, master sommelier, 1856 – Culinary Residence, Auburn

“In my estimation, most Sauvignon Blanc is overrated, and Sancerre mania has made the appellation’s name a substitute for exercising any real discernment among its wines. But if pressed, I’d point you toward Hippolyte Reverdy, a family domaine whose Sancerre gives you something to appreciate beyond name recognition and ease of pronunciation. It’s bright and floral, with citrus, a stony finish, and enough texture from a short spell on the lees to smooth out its texture. Drink it with oysters, fresh goat cheese, or a simple green salad.” —Bodhi Landa, sommelier-at-large, Bar Etienne, New York City

“The Quincy region in Loire Valley is an expression not nearly enough people are talking about. While Sancerre gets most of the attention, Quincy was actually one of the first French appellations to receive AOC status. It offers many of the same qualities found in higher-priced Sancerre and Pouilly-Fumé, with vibrant citrus, minerality, and a crisp, refreshing finish.” —Brianna Ellis, general manager, Tannin Bar, Park City, Utah

“Pepper Bridge Winery makes a Sauvignon Blanc that deserves far more attention than it gets. It is new on my list and becoming a staff pick! It balances bright citrus and crisp acidity beautifully, while offering enough texture and subtle richness to make it work at our table. For me, it’s a great example of how the Pacific Northwest can produce Sauvignon Blanc with both freshness and depth.” —Owen Perry, wine director, Lansdowne, Portland

“For me, Sauvignon Blanc from Elgin, South Africa deserves far more recognition for its balance of aromatic intensity and restraint. The region’s cool climate lends freshness and precision to the finest examples, where vivid citrus fruit, vibrant acidity, and subtle flinty notes bring both energy and depth. Paul Clüver Sauvignon Blanc 2025 is a compelling introduction, combining gooseberry, passion fruit, and fresh herbal notes with a saline edge and a textured palate. A small proportion of Sémillon adds fullness while preserving freshness, making it a beautiful companion to seafood.” —Cornelia Duchessa, wine director, BRASS, NYC

“One of the most underrated Sauvignon Blancs is without question from Menetou-Salon in the Loire Valley, just outside of the wildly popular appellation of Sancerre. The wines, specifically from Paul-Henry Pellé in the village of Morogues, come from soils rich in Kimmeridgian limestone and are some of the most nuanced Sauvignons out there. The specific bottle I love is the Pellé’s Menetou-Salon ‘Morogues Blanchais’ 2023.” —Francesco Grosso, wine director, Ai Fiori, NYC

“In a world where the biggest argument is whether New Zealand Sauvignon Blanc, with its grassy and gooseberry flavors, or California’s expression, offering notes of peach and tropical fruit, is the most sought after, it’s easy to overlook some of the original Sauvignon Blancs from France’s Loire Valley. These wines bring a strong minerality and vibrant notes of citrus, particularly lime and lemon.They are a magical pairing with seafood dishes, especially those finished with a squeeze of lemon. They are also incredible alongside fatty dishes, such as duck breast or creamy sauces, where their high acidity balances the richness. Domaine Durand Sancerre is a perfect example of how beautifully this style can shine.” —Lee Nevarez, sommelier, The National, Autograph Collection, Oklahoma City

content:
Bordeaux put the idea of fine wine on the map. The 1855 Classification became a model for identifying quality wines and producers, a concept copied throughout the region, as well as the world over.

But anyone who’s been to Bordeaux knows that those Classified Growths don’t reflect how dynamic and forward-thinking Bordeaux is today. The vast region is populated with family-run estates, organic growers, and new generations eager to put their stamp on a style. And while a changing climate and society have given Bordeaux hard knocks, the sensational headlines don’t fully reflect what’s really going on in a legacy region that’s entering its next chapter.

For those interested in getting to know the modern Bordeaux landscape, we compiled a list of producers showcasing what the region has to offer right now. From historic châteaux ranked in the region’s highest classifications to experimental producers working with amphora aging, here are eight producers to know to get into Bordeaux.

Château Troplong Mondot

Founded in 1700, Troplong Mondot is ranked Premier Grand Cru Classé in the St. Émilion Classification, which was established in 1955. Being located on the Right Bank, Merlot dominates the cuvées, with a touch of Cabernet Sauvignon and Cabernet Franc rounding out the style. Sustainability is the keyword for this St. Émilion estate. The B Corp-certified winery pledges to cut carbon emissions in half by 2030, reaching net zero by 2050. The Grand Vin ranges in price depending on vintage, anywhere from $120 upwards, but like most Bordeaux châteaux, it offers an affordable second label, Mondot.

Château Malartic-Lagravière

Located in Pessac-Léognan, Malartic-Lagravière was one of six estates to be classified for both its red and white wines in the 1953 Graves Classification. Gravel, shell limestone, and clay define the soils. Cabernet Sauvignon dominates the red wines, with Cabernet Franc and Merlot completing the blend. Out of the 180 acres of vineyards, 17 acres are dedicated to Sauvignon Blanc and Semillon. The white wines, such as the flagship Malartic-Lagraviére Blanc, retailing at around $90 are some of the most exciting in all of Bordeaux, with lots of bright acidity and lifted aromatics.

Château Durfort-Vivens

Durfort-Vivens may be a Second Growth in the 1855 Classification, but the Margaux estate is one of the most innovative operators in Bordeaux today. Instead of oak, owners Gonzague and Claire Lurton only use amphoras in the cellar, which they believe brings out the best expression of their Cabernet-focused wines. While Bordeaux is best known for blending different parcels, the couple experiments with single-vineyard expressions. In addition to their Bordeaux property, they own Acaibo winery in Sonoma, bringing another dimension to their knowledge of Cabernet.

Château Pontet-Canet

Pontet-Canet, in the Pauillac appellation, is a leader in biodynamic viticulture. Originally founded in 1781, the Fifth Growth château was purchased by the Tesseron family in 1975. In the 1990s, they converted to biodynamics, a rarity in the region, and paved the way for other estates. In 2015, Justine Tesseron took over, in partnership with her brother, Noé, and their cousins. The family also owns the Napa estate Pym-Rae, which was the former home of actor Robin Williams. There, they continue their biodynamic farming principles and focus on Cabernet-based wines.

Château Lagrange

This St. Julien Third Growth estate prides itself on its 265-acre contiguous vineyard in the appellation’s gravelly soils. Founded in the 1700s, it counts Thomas Jefferson among its celebrity clients. It enjoyed a reputation as a fine wine producer until the late 1800s, when phylloxera, world wars, and other hardships decimated the property. In 1983, Keizo Saji from the Suntory family purchased Lagrange and invested heavily in restorations, notably subdividing the vineyard into 103 plots and taking a detailed approach to grape cultivation. The château produces three red wines at various price points, along with two whites, making this an ideal estate to get into Bordeaux.

Château Haut-Brion

One of the original First Growths in the 1855 Classification, Haut-Brion is one of the most well-known and collected Bordeaux wines. (If opportunity presents itself, it’s worth getting to know all of the First Growths, but Haut-Brion has a fun story to get into.) The reds are led by Cabernet Sauvignon, with Merlot and Cabernet Franc also in the composition. The white wine, a blend of Sauvignon Blanc and Semillon, is an IYKYK wine. Overseeing Haut-Brion and its parent company, Domaine Clarence Dillon, is Prince Robert of Luxembourg, who, before taking over the family estate, worked as a screenwriter in Los Angeles. He wants to bring new drinkers into the Bordeaux fold and, 20 years ago, created the Clarendelle wines, an affordable, lifestyle-driven line. While a bottle of Haut-Brion Grand Vin red might go for $450-plus depending on the vintage, drinkers looking for an entry point to these storied wines can find the Clarendelle for $23.

Château Angélus

Merlot dominates many of the wines in the Right Bank, but Château Angelus in St. Émilion puts Cabernet Franc front and center. The vineyard, a south-facing amphitheater, contains sandy-limestone soils at lower elevations, which is ideal for Cab Franc, while Merlot vines thrive in the heavier clay soils up-slope. Earlier this year, the estate unveiled a new wine cellar, which took 14 years to construct. If the Grand Vin, which can go for $400 or more depending on vintage, is out of budget, the estate also produces second and third labels for a more affordable taste. The second wine, Le Carillon de Angelus, retails for an average of $150, and the third wine, No. 3 d’Angelus, is priced at approximately $60.

Château d’Yquem

Red and white wines are only part of the story; Bordeaux is also the home of Sauternes, one of the most famous sweet wines in the world. In order to create these dessert sips, vintners rely on botrytis, or noble rot, to concentrate sugars in the grapes. Long considered the pinnacle of Sauternes producer, Château d’Yquem’s laborious process requires a careful selection of grapes during harvest, as they believe various levels of botrytis create the ultimate expression of Sauternes. The estate has been certified organic since 2022, which is no small feat considering the same humidity needed for botrytis development challenges general viticulture, with its heightened risk of bad rot. While even half-bottles can retail for $300, it’s worth the investment to understand the art and science of botrytized wines.
